1 Peter 1.summary: Peter greets Christians scattered across several regions of Asia Minor, calling them God's chosen 'exiles' (1 Peter 1:1-2). He praises God for the 'living hope' given through Jesus' resurrection and for an inheritance that cannot perish, kept safe for them while God guards them through faith (1 Peter 1:3-5). Their present trials, he says, are real but temporary, and they test the genuineness of faith the way fire tests gold; though they have not seen Jesus, they love him and rejoice (1 Peter 1:6-9). The salvation they now enjoy was something the prophets searched and angels long to look into 1 Peter 1:10-12. On that basis Peter calls them to prepare their minds, set their hope fully on grace, and be holy in all their conduct, because God is holy (1 Peter 1:13-16). They were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 'like that of a lamb without blemish or spot,' who was known before the world's foundation and made known in the last times for their sake (1 Peter 1:17-21). Having been made new by the 'living and abiding word of God,' they are to love one another earnestly from the heart (1 Peter 1:22-25).
1 Peter 1.whereWeAre:
The readers were undergoing 'various trials' and being 'grieved.' The chapter does not specify what the trials were, though later chapters mention insults and slander (2:12, 3:16, 4:4, 4:14) and a 'fiery trial' (4:12).

The churches addressed seem to have included many people who once lived by pagan customs ('the passions of your former ignorance,' 1:14; 'futile ways inherited from your forefathers,' 1:18). Some Jewish Christians may also have been among them. The letter does not identify the proportions.

The gospel had reached these regions through preaching (1:12, 1:25). The New Testament mentions people from Pontus, Cappadocia and Asia among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9-10) and Paul's work in Asia (Acts 19), but the letter does not say how these specific communities began.

No empire-wide law against Christianity is documented for the first century; the evidence is of local, case-by-case action (Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Pliny, Letters 10.96-97). Nero is recorded by the Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 15.44) as having punished Christians in Rome after the great fire of AD 64. Whether the suffering in 1 Peter is local social hostility or official action is debated, and the chapter itself does not say. The letter's opening gives hope and identity to people who were suffering social pressure for their faith. The 'exile' language, the contrast between the readers' present trials and future glory, and the call to holiness all speak to Christians who no longer shared their neighbors' way of life and paid a price for it.

keyFigures.name: Peter
keyFigures.role: Greets the readers, praises God for salvation, and urges them to hope, holiness and love. His apostolic voice gives the letter its authority and pastoral tone.

keyFigures.name: The elect exiles in Asia Minor
keyFigures.role: They are the people being encouraged, reminded of their identity, and called to holiness and love. The whole chapter is addressed to them as chosen people under pressure who need hope.

keyFigures.name: God the Father
keyFigures.role: Source of mercy, new birth, inheritance and protection. The chapter's hope rests on what the Father has done in Christ.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: The one through whom believers have hope, redemption and faith in God. His sufferings and glory are the center of the prophets' message and of the readers' hope.

keyFigures.name: The Holy Spirit / the Spirit of Christ
keyFigures.role: Sanctifies the readers, inspired the prophets, and empowers the preachers of the good news. Shows that the Father, Son and Spirit are all involved in salvation, a pattern many Christians describe in Trinitarian terms; the text does not use that term.

keyFigures.name: The Old Testament prophets
keyFigures.role: They foretold the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow, and learned that they were serving future believers. Connects the readers' experience to the long story of God's promises.

keyFigures.name: Angels
keyFigures.role: Mentioned to show how remarkable the gospel is. Underlines the value of the salvation the readers have received.

keyFigures.name: Those who preached the good news to the readers
keyFigures.role: They announced the gospel 'by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven.'. Shows that the readers' faith began with the preaching of the word.

keyFigures.name: The readers' forefathers
keyFigures.role: Represent the former way of life from which the readers were ransomed. Helps show the cost of redemption and the break from the past.

keyFigures.name: Isaiah
keyFigures.role: His words are quoted to affirm the lasting power of God's word. Shows the writer grounding his message in the Old Testament.

keyFigures.name: Israel at the exodus (the Passover lamb background)
keyFigures.role: Provide background imagery for the chapter's teaching. Many interpreters see Passover and sacrificial imagery behind the verse; the text does not state the connection directly.

keyThemes.theme: Living hope rooted in the resurrection
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers have been born again 'to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,' and are told to set their hope fully on the grace to come.

Christian hope is grounded in the resurrection of Jesus, which gives a reason to endure present difficulty.

keyThemes.theme: Joy and refinement through suffering
keyThemes.explanation:
Trials are described as temporary and as tests of the genuineness of faith, comparable to fire refining gold, leading to praise and honor at Christ's revelation. Believers rejoice even though they have not seen Jesus.

Faith can be strengthened and proved genuine under pressure, and joy and grief can exist side by side.

keyThemes.theme: Chosen, protected and heirs
keyThemes.explanation:
The readers are called elect, born again, and heirs of an imperishable inheritance, and God's power guards them through faith.

Identity and security rest on God's action and promise, not on social standing.

keyThemes.theme: Holiness as the response to redemption
keyThemes.explanation:
Because God is holy and because believers were ransomed at the cost of Christ's precious blood, they are to leave their former passions behind and live in reverent fear of the Father.

Grace and gratitude, not mere rule-keeping, are the foundation for a changed life.

keyThemes.theme: Love for one another and the enduring word
keyThemes.explanation:
Obeying the truth purifies the soul for sincere brotherly love, and new birth comes through the 'living and abiding word of God,' which outlasts everything human.

A community formed by God's word is meant to show earnest, heartfelt love.

explainedReferences.explanation: Peter quotes the command to be holy because God is holy.
Peter quotes the command to be holy because God is holy.
Peter quotes Isaiah's words about grass withering while God's word endures.

1 Peter 2.summary: Peter tells his readers to lay aside malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander, and to long for pure spiritual milk like newborn infants, so that they may grow up into salvation (1 Peter 2:1-3). Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen and precious to God, they themselves are built up as living stones into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood that offers spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:4-5). Old Testament passages about a cornerstone show that those who believe will not be put to shame, while those who do not believe stumble (1 Peter 2:6-8). The readers are described with titles once used of Israel: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, who once were not a people but now are God's people (1 Peter 2:9-10). As sojourners and exiles they are to live honorably among the Gentiles so that outsiders who slander them may see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:11-12). They are told to submit to human authorities, including the emperor and governors, as free people who serve God (1 Peter 2:13-17), and household servants are told to submit to their masters, even harsh ones (1 Peter 2:18-20). The chapter closes by pointing to Christ's suffering as an example and as the means by which sins are borne and wounds healed, so that those who were straying sheep have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls (1 Peter 2:21-25).
1 Peter 2.whereWeAre:
Christians were being spoken against as 'evildoers' by their Gentile neighbors (2:12). The chapter does not say what they were accused of.

Ancient sources show that early Christians were sometimes accused of atheism (for not worshiping the gods), of disloyalty, or of immoral behavior. The Roman governor Pliny, writing to the emperor Trajan around AD 112 about Christians in Bithynia-Pontus, a region addressed in 1 Peter 1:1, treats the 'name' of Christian as a matter for punishment. That is later than the usual dates proposed for 1 Peter, so it shows what could happen in the region, not the situation of these readers.

Enslaved and servant populations were a significant part of the Roman economy and household. Some members of the churches were household servants (2:18). Many Roman households were headed by a master whose religion the household was expected to follow.

Roman governors had authority to punish wrongdoers; 2:14 describes them as sent by the emperor to punish evildoers and praise those who do good. The call to submit, honor and do good makes sense for a vulnerable minority whose reputation was damaged. The instructions to servants are addressed to people with little legal power. The 'exile' language gives them a way of understanding their social position.

keyFigures.name: Christ (the living stone, the Shepherd and Overseer)
keyFigures.role: Foundation of the community, model for conduct and the one who brings healing. Everything in the chapter's instructions is tied to who he is and what he has done.

keyFigures.name: The believing community (living stones, a holy priesthood, God's people)
keyFigures.role: They are addressed with their identity and their calling to proclaim God's excellencies and live honorably. The chapter shows how a minority community can understand itself as belonging to God.

keyFigures.name: Those who do not believe (the builders who rejected the stone)
keyFigures.role: They contrast with believers; they stumble because they disobey the word. Shows that Christ divides people into those who trust him and those who reject him.

keyFigures.name: The Gentiles (outsiders)
keyFigures.role: The audience for the believers' public conduct. The chapter wants believers' behavior to answer slander and, if possible, lead to praise of God.

keyFigures.name: The emperor and governors
keyFigures.role: Readers are told to submit to them and honor the emperor, and are told that governors punish evildoers and praise those who do good. Shows the writer's expectation that Christians would be good citizens within Roman society.

keyFigures.name: Household servants
keyFigures.role: They are addressed directly and told to submit and to endure unjust suffering. Christ's example in suffering is offered to them in a particular way.

keyFigures.name: Masters
keyFigures.role: Mentioned as those the servants are to respect. The passage does not give instructions to masters here.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: The one to whom the community belongs and to whom they answer. Behind the chapter's commands is the idea that believers live before God.

keyFigures.name: Straying sheep
keyFigures.role: Closes the chapter with an image of restoration. Echoes Isaiah 53:6 and Old Testament shepherd imagery.

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Background for how the letter describes the church. Shows continuity with the Old Testament, though interpreters differ on how to explain the relationship.

keyThemes.theme: Growth through longing for God's word
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are called to put away destructive attitudes and long for 'pure spiritual milk' so that they may grow up in salvation, having tasted that the Lord is good.

Spiritual growth involves both leaving behind what harms community and regularly seeking what nourishes faith.

keyThemes.theme: A people with a new identity
keyThemes.explanation:
The readers are living stones in a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, a chosen race, a holy nation and God's own people, who have received mercy.

Identity as God's people comes from God's choice and mercy, and carries a calling to proclaim his excellencies.

keyThemes.theme: Honorable conduct as witness
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to live so honorably among their critics that their good deeds may lead others to glorify God, and are to submit to authority and honor everyone as free people who serve God.

Good conduct and respect can answer slander and show that faith is not a threat, though the text doesn't promise that critics will be convinced.

keyThemes.theme: Enduring unjust suffering after Christ's example
keyThemes.explanation:
Servants, and by extension all believers, are told that patiently enduring unjust suffering is commendable before God, because Christ suffered and did not retaliate.

Christ's response to mistreatment offers a pattern; the passage does not say that suffering abuse is itself a good, or that injustice should be accepted without limit.

keyThemes.theme: Christ's saving work: healing and return to the Shepherd
keyThemes.explanation:
Christ bore sins in his body on the tree, so that believers may die to sin and live to righteousness; they are healed by his wounds and have returned to the Shepherd.

Christ's death both forgives and enables a changed life.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: These passages quote the declaration about trusting in the cornerstone in Zion.
The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is directly quoted.
Peter quotes the statement that no deceit was found in his mouth.

1 Peter 3.summary: Peter continues his instructions for life in a hostile society. He tells wives to be subject to their husbands so that even husbands who do not obey the word may be won 'without a word' by their wives' conduct, and he points them to the 'hidden person of the heart' and a gentle, quiet spirit as true adornment, with Sarah as an example 1 Peter 3:1-6. He tells husbands to live with their wives in an understanding way and to honor them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered (1 Peter 3:7). He then addresses the whole community: be united, sympathetic, loving and humble, and do not repay evil for evil but bless, using words from Psalm 34 1 Peter 3:8-12. Suffering for doing good is not to be feared; believers are to honor Christ as Lord, be ready to give a gentle and respectful answer for their hope, and keep a good conscience, since it is better to suffer for doing good than for doing wrong (1 Peter 3:13-17). The ground for this is Christ, who suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God, and who was made alive in the spirit; the passage mentions his proclamation to 'spirits in prison' from the days of Noah, compares the flood to baptism, and ends with Christ's resurrection, ascension and rule over angels, authorities and powers (1 Peter 3:18-22).
1 Peter 3.whereWeAre:
Some Christian wives were married to men who did not believe, and the passage assumes that their faith could cause tension in the household.

Christians were being reviled for their good conduct (3:16) and might suffer for righteousness (3:14). The passage does not say what form this took.

Roman writers of the time, such as Plutarch in his marriage advice, expected wives to worship their husbands' gods and to avoid foreign cults. This helps explain why a wife's different faith might be controversial.

Wealthy Roman women were sometimes criticized by moralists for elaborate hairstyles and costly jewelry and clothing, and similar warnings appear in other Jewish and Christian writings. Whether this was a problem in these specific churches is not stated. The wife-husband instructions address a real tension: how to live faithfully when a spouse does not share one's faith. The call to bless rather than retaliate and to give a gentle answer fits a community under verbal pressure. The Noah reference may have resonated with readers who were a small minority, though the text does not say so.

keyFigures.name: Christian wives
keyFigures.role: They are addressed first, and are told to be subject, to keep respectful and pure conduct, and to focus on inner beauty. The chapter recognizes that some of them faced religious division at home.

keyFigures.name: Husbands, including non-believing husbands
keyFigures.role: The first group may be won by conduct; the second group is told to show honor to their wives. The letter addresses both mixed-faith and Christian households.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Provides an example of respectful conduct. The text says she 'obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.'. Anchors the instruction in Old Testament models.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Mentioned only as the one Sarah called 'lord.' A limited role in the chapter.

keyFigures.name: The believing community as a whole
keyFigures.role: They are told to be like-minded, loving and humble, to bless in return for reviling, and to be ready to explain their hope. The chapter's ethic is meant to mark the whole community.

keyFigures.name: Those who revile the readers' good behavior
keyFigures.role: They may be put to shame by the readers' good conduct. Part of the pressure the readers were under.

keyFigures.name: Christ
keyFigures.role: The ground for the readers' hope and endurance. He suffered once for sins, was made alive, proclaimed to spirits, rose, ascended and is at God's right hand. Everything in the chapter's second half rests on him.

keyFigures.name: The spirits in prison
keyFigures.role: The recipients of Christ's proclamation. A debated detail in the passage; the surrounding point is Christ's victory and the pattern of judgment and rescue.

keyFigures.name: Noah and the eight in the ark
keyFigures.role: Presented as those brought safely through water, which corresponds to baptism. Used to illustrate rescue through judgment.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Source of blessing, patient with the disobedient, and the one to whom believers are brought. Provides the basis for their confidence.

keyFigures.name: Angels, authorities and powers
keyFigures.role: They show the extent of his rule. Reassures readers that no power is above Christ.

keyFigures.name: David (the psalmist)
keyFigures.role: Source of the quoted words. Shows the writer using the Psalms to support practical teaching.

keyThemes.theme: Winning others by conduct and inner character
keyThemes.explanation:
Wives married to unbelieving husbands are told that their pure and respectful behavior can win them 'without a word,' and that inner beauty is precious to God.

The way believers live can speak persuasively, and character matters more than appearance.

keyThemes.theme: Honor and shared standing within the household
keyThemes.explanation:
Husbands are to live in an understanding way with their wives and honor them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.

Spiritual equality calls for honor and consideration in how people treat each other.

keyThemes.theme: Blessing instead of retaliation
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to be united, sympathetic and humble, and are not to repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but to bless, because they were called to inherit a blessing.

Responding to insult with blessing breaks the cycle of retaliation.

keyThemes.theme: Ready, gentle witness and a clear conscience
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are told to set Christ apart as Lord in their hearts, to be ready to explain their hope with gentleness and respect, and to keep a good conscience.

Being ready to explain one's hope should be paired with humility and respect.

keyThemes.theme: Christ's suffering, vindication and rule
keyThemes.explanation:
Christ suffered once for sins, was made alive, proclaimed to spirits, rose, ascended and rules over all powers; baptism is linked to the flood and to his resurrection.

Christ's path of suffering followed by victory gives hope to those who suffer for doing good.

explainedReferences.explanation: Peter quotes the psalm's instructions about speech, peace, and the righteous.

1 Peter 4.summary: Because Christ suffered in the flesh, Peter tells his readers to arm themselves with the same way of thinking, since whoever has suffered in the flesh has finished with sin, and to live no longer by human passions but by God's will (1 Peter 4:1-2). They have spent enough time doing what the Gentiles want to do; former friends are surprised that they no longer join in and so they malign them, but those people will give account to the one who is ready to judge the living and the dead (1 Peter 4:3-5). The chapter says the gospel was preached even to those who are dead (1 Peter 4:6). Since the end of all things is at hand, believers are to be self-controlled and sober-minded for prayer, to love one another earnestly because love covers a multitude of sins, to show hospitality without grumbling, and to use their gifts to serve one another so that God may be glorified in everything (1 Peter 4:7-11). They should not be surprised at the 'fiery trial,' but rejoice in sharing Christ's sufferings; to be insulted for the name of Christ is a blessing, but no one should suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer or meddler (1 Peter 4:12-15). To suffer 'as a Christian' is no shame; judgment begins with God's household, and those who suffer according to God's will should entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while continuing to do good (1 Peter 4:16-19).
1 Peter 4.whereWeAre:
The readers' former friends were surprised that the believers no longer shared in their activities and so maligned them.

The readers were undergoing a 'fiery trial' and were being insulted for the name of Christ. The text suggests the possibility of more severe suffering, but does not describe it in detail.

The Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 15.44) says that Nero punished Christians in Rome after the fire of AD 64, and that the name 'Christians' was in use. This shows the name was known and could bring danger by that time in Rome. It does not show that the same thing was happening in Asia Minor.

Around AD 112, the governor Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan from Bithynia-Pontus about how to handle people accused of being Christians, and said that persistent Christians were to be punished. This is later than the likely date of 1 Peter and shows what could happen in the same region. The chapter reflects a community whose faith had cost them social ties and whose critics were hostile. The Christian name was becoming a public label that could bring trouble. The chapter's guidance to avoid wrongdoing, to love and serve, and to trust God applies to a minority that could not assume protection.

keyFigures.name: Christ
keyFigures.role: The model and basis for believers' endurance, and the one through whom God is glorified. The chapter ties every instruction to sharing in Christ's sufferings and future glory.

keyFigures.name: The readers (believers in the churches)
keyFigures.role: They are told to change their lives, love one another, serve with their gifts, and endure fiery trials. The chapter is about how a community under pressure should live.

keyFigures.name: The Gentiles / former companions
keyFigures.role: They are surprised by the readers' changed behavior and malign them. Explains the source of the readers' social tension.

keyFigures.name: The living and the dead
keyFigures.role: Everyone will give account to God. Establishes that no one escapes God's judgment and that the readers' critics will answer to him.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: The one to whom believers entrust their souls. Provides the grounds for hope and endurance.

keyFigures.name: The Spirit of glory and of God
keyFigures.role: A sign of God's presence in suffering. Gives comfort to those who are reviled.

keyFigures.name: Murderers, thieves, evildoers and meddlers
keyFigures.role: A contrast to suffering 'as a Christian.' Insists that any suffering believers face should be for Christ, not for wrongdoing.

keyFigures.name: Those who do not obey the gospel
keyFigures.role: Contrasted with believers in the discussion of judgment. Underlines the seriousness of the gospel message.

keyFigures.name: Noah's generation and the 'spirits in prison' of chapter 3
keyFigures.role: Background to a debated verse. Interpreters link the passages in different ways.

keyThemes.theme: A changed life in place of the old way
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to live for God's will rather than human passions, having spent enough time on the lifestyle of their former companions. This change leads to misunderstanding and slander.

A commitment to Christ often means leaving habits and social patterns behind, and it can be misunderstood.

keyThemes.theme: Love, hospitality and serving with one's gifts
keyThemes.explanation:
In light of the end being near, believers are to pray, love earnestly, welcome each other without grumbling and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.

Ordinary acts of service and welcome are a way of glorifying God.

keyThemes.theme: Suffering as sharing in Christ's sufferings
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers should not be surprised by fiery trials, but rejoice because they are sharing Christ's sufferings, and the Spirit of glory rests on them.

Suffering for Christ is not a sign of God's absence.

keyThemes.theme: Suffering for the right reasons
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers must not suffer as wrongdoers; suffering 'as a Christian' is no cause for shame.

The reason for suffering matters; wrongdoing is not persecution.

keyThemes.theme: God's judgment and trust in the faithful Creator
keyThemes.explanation:
Judgment begins with God's household, and the outcome for those who reject the gospel is more serious. Those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator and keep doing good.

Believers can face uncertainty with trust in God's faithfulness while continuing to do good.

explainedReferences.explanation: Peter quotes the proverb contrasting the righteous person's salvation and the ungodly person's fate.

1 Peter 5.summary: Peter, as a 'fellow elder' and witness of Christ's sufferings who shares in the glory to be revealed, urges the elders among his readers to shepherd God's flock willingly rather than under compulsion, eagerly rather than for shameful gain, and as examples rather than by domineering; when the Chief Shepherd appears they will receive an unfading crown of glory (1 Peter 5:1-4). Younger people are to be subject to the elders, and all are to clothe themselves with humility toward one another, since 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' (1 Peter 5:5). Believers are to humble themselves under God's mighty hand, trusting him to lift them up at the proper time, and to cast all their anxieties on him because he cares for them (1 Peter 5:6-7). They are to be sober-minded and watchful because their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion, and they are to resist him, firm in faith, knowing their fellow believers around the world are going through the same sufferings (1 Peter 5:8-9). After a brief time of suffering, the God of all grace will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them (1 Peter 5:10-11). Peter closes by saying he wrote briefly through Silvanus, sending greetings from the church in 'Babylon' and from Mark, urging a kiss of love, and wishing peace on all who are in Christ (1 Peter 5:12-14).
1 Peter 5.whereWeAre:
Local churches were led by elders, a role seen elsewhere in Acts and the letters (Acts 14:23; 20:17-28; Titus 1:5). The letter shows these leaders being instructed about motives and style of leadership.

Christians in the provinces were suffering, and the author says that believers around the world were undergoing similar experiences (5:9). The letter does not describe the details or scope.

Early Christian tradition places Peter in Rome and connects him with Mark; this tradition is old, but it is not itself a first-century document, and so the connection of 'Babylon' with Rome is an inference supported by the tradition and by the use of 'Babylon' in other Jewish and Christian writings.

Jewish writers after AD 70 sometimes used 'Babylon' to refer to Rome, since both had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple (compare 2 Baruch and 4 Ezra). This is later than the likely date of 1 Peter if Peter wrote it, though some think the usage was already established by then. The call for humble shepherding responds to the needs of churches under pressure, where leadership could be tested by hardship. The warning about the devil and the assurance of restoration are linked to the broader suffering described throughout the letter. The closing greetings show a network of relationships among early Christian leaders.

keyFigures.name: Peter
keyFigures.role: Exhorts the elders and the community, and concludes the letter. His self-description as 'fellow elder' shows a pastoral tone rather than a distant authority.

keyFigures.name: The elders
keyFigures.role: They are told how to lead: as shepherds, willingly, eagerly and by example. The chapter gives early teaching on the character of church leadership.

keyFigures.name: The younger ones
keyFigures.role: They are told to be subject to the elders. Shows that humility is expected in both directions.

keyFigures.name: The flock of God
keyFigures.role: The people whom the elders shepherd. Applies the Old Testament image of God's people as a flock.

keyFigures.name: The Chief Shepherd (Christ)
keyFigures.role: He will reward faithful elders with an unfading crown of glory. Reminds elders that they serve under him.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: The one to whom believers humble themselves and entrust their anxieties. The chapter ends with confidence that God will restore and establish his people.

keyFigures.name: The devil (the adversary)
keyFigures.role: The opponent believers are to resist. Shows a spiritual dimension to the pressures the readers face.

keyFigures.name: Fellow believers throughout the world
keyFigures.role: Their shared experience encourages the readers. Connects local suffering to a worldwide community.

keyFigures.name: Silvanus
keyFigures.role: Helped write or deliver the letter. His role is a clue to the letter's composition, which is debated.

keyFigures.name: 'She who is at Babylon' (the church there)
keyFigures.role: Sends greetings. Offers a possible clue to where the letter was written.

keyFigures.name: Mark
keyFigures.role: Sends greetings. Early tradition connects him with Peter, but the letter does not describe their relationship in detail.

keyFigures.name: Those who are in Christ
keyFigures.role: Receive the final wish for peace. Closes the letter by identifying the community by its relationship to Christ.

keyFigures.name: Nero and Roman authorities
keyFigures.role: Background only. Offered for context, not as part of the text.

keyThemes.theme: Servant leadership
keyThemes.explanation:
Elders are to shepherd willingly and eagerly, not for gain, and not by domineering, but as examples, knowing they serve under the Chief Shepherd.

Those with responsibility are to lead through example and care, not control or self-interest.

keyThemes.theme: Humility before God and one another
keyThemes.explanation:
Everyone is to clothe themselves with humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, and to humble themselves under God's mighty hand.

Humility is the proper posture toward God and one another.

keyThemes.theme: Trusting God with anxiety
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are told to cast all their anxieties on God because he cares for them.

God invites people to bring their worries to him, trusting his care.

keyThemes.theme: Spiritual watchfulness and steadfast resistance
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to be sober-minded and watchful against the devil, who prowls like a lion, and to resist him, firm in faith, knowing others suffer too.

Alertness and faith, not fear, are the proper response to spiritual opposition.

keyThemes.theme: God's restoring grace after brief suffering
keyThemes.explanation:
The God of all grace, who called believers to eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them after they have suffered a little while.

Present suffering is real but limited, and God is the one who sustains and completes his people.

explainedReferences.explanation: Peter quotes the saying about grace to the humble.
